citing ADAPSO, Judge Tatel explained “the agency’s decision . . . must be 
supported by substantial evidence—otherwise it would be arbitrary and 
capricious.” Reiterating the reasoning of ADAPSO, the court observed that 
“[t]he difference between this informal adjudication and a formal adjudication 
on the record is thus not the amount of evidence the agency must provide to 
support its decision, but where the evidence may be found.” That was because, 
“[i]n an adjudication on the record ‘substantial evidence [must] be found within 
the record of closed-record proceedings,’ while in an informal adjudication the 
agency can provide the court with any evidence it had before it when it made 
its decision.” The court ultimately concluded that “the agency’s decision to 
treat” the two kinds of products “differently finds no support in the evidence 
the agency considered” and was thus “arbitrary and capricious.”
Many other courts of appeals appear to agree with ADAPSO"s approach. 
See, e.g., Amin v. Afayorkas, 24 F.4th 383, 393 (5th Cir. 2022); Sevoian v. 
Aschroft, 290 F.3d 166, 174 (3d Cir. 2002); Olenhouse v. Commodity Credit 
Corp., 42 F.3d 1560, 1575 (10th Cir. 1994). But periodically, courts will 
examine the standards of review from organic statutes, distinguishing between 
“substantial evidence” and “arbitrary and capricious” review in a specific 
context. See, e.g.. Labor Council for Latin American Advancement v. EPA, 12 
F.4th 234, 245 n.l (2d Cir. 2021) (reasoning that the “substantial evidence” 
standard in the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) is “particularly 
dAmanding^' and “distinct” from the APA’s standard); Chemical Manufacturers 
Assn. V. EPA, 859 F.2d 977, 991 (D.C. Cir. 1988) (“Congress perceived some 
difference between the standard it chose for TSCA and the APA’s arbitrary- 
and-capricious standard.”); Corrosion Proof Fittings v. EPA, 947 F.2d 1201, 
1214 (5th Cir. 1991).
3. 
What Did the APA’s Authors Intend? In ADAPSO, then-Judge Scalia 
quoted the following passage from Professor Kenneth Culp Davis’s treatise on 
administrative law: “Does the extent of required factual support for rules 
depend in part on whether the standard for review is ‘substantial evidence’ or 
‘arbitrary and capricious’? Although from 1946 until some time during the 
1970s the dominant answer probably was yes, a change to a no answer has 
probably occurred during the 1970s . . . .” 1 KENNETH CULP Da v is , 
Ad min is t r a t iv e La w Tr e a t is e § 6:13, at 512 (2d ed. 1978). Assuming the 
factual predicate of Professor Davis’s claim (that the meaning of these 
standards somehow changed between the 1940s and 1970s), would a modem 
court be justified in applying the newer understanding? Or should the 
understanding of the APA’s authors control?
